Front-end nodes route requests and coordinate 2PC, storage nodes talk to MySQL with read-only replicas serving snapshot reads, and a control plane of storage control, a placement registry and a rebalancing keeper moves ranges with only seconds of unavailability, so 5 percent more data needs roughly 5 percent more hardware. The authors explain why FoundationDB, Vitess and CockroachDB were rejected, including FoundationDB testing out at 500 single-threaded storage processes against clusters with more than 10,000 cores, and CockroachDB's quorum replication adding about 80 ms of inter-region write latency versus MySQL semi-sync. Randomized simulation testing found tens of bugs including deadlocks and range-transfer data corruption, and the post reports qualitative rather than numeric outcomes.
title: Future-proofing our metadata stack with Panda, a scalable key-value store

keyTakeaways: Place tenants by data size and usage, not tenant count, or heavy tenants pile onto the same shard by accident.
Simulate a rebalancing plan before executing it, so you can see the predicted spread instead of discovering it in production.
Batch copy plus binlog tailing keeps the tenant live on the source until lag is seconds, leaving only a short cutover to protect.
A multi-reader single-writer lock that the mover must acquire within a deadline turns a risky cutover into a safe, failable step.
Run verifiers before, during and after a move, and formally model the copy algorithm if correctness is load bearing.
summary: Shopify runs isolated pods, each with its own MySQL shard plus Redis and Memcached, and routes every request by shop ID through a routing table, but new merchants were assigned to arbitrary shards and uneven growth left resource-heavy shops clustered together, so the least used and most used shard varied by almost four times. The team built shard balancing that places shops by data size and usage rather than count, and the post reports that simulating a proposed set of moves brought the spread between least and most used shards closer to two times. Moves run through Ghostferry, Shopify's open-source tool, in three phases: batch-copy each table's rows for a shop_id in separate transactions using SELECT FOR UPDATE while simultaneously tailing and filtering the row-based binlog onto the target, cut over once replay lag is on the order of seconds by taking a Redis-backed writer lock that blocks shop writes and replaying the final binlog coordinate, then update the routing table to the new pod, release the lock and prune stale source data. If the mover cannot get the writer lock in time the move simply fails rather than risking data loss. Verifiers run before, during and after each move to check completeness and corruption, and Ghostferry's core algorithm is modeled in a TLA+ specification; the post describes the result as virtually zero consumer-facing downtime without giving a measured cutover duration.
title: Shard Balancing: Moving Shops Confidently with Zero-Downtime at Terabyte-scale

keyTakeaways: Colocating code with its database removes the network hop, so the N+1 query pattern stops being a performance trap.
Output gates let writes stay non-blocking while still being safe: hold the response until the write is confirmed, or replace it with an error.
Intercepting the SQLite WAL through a VFS turns a local embedded database into a replicated, durable one without changing the query layer.
Confirming a commit on 3 of 5 followers in different data centers buys durability without waiting on object storage.
Keeping the log for 30 days after a snapshot gives point-in-time recovery almost for free, since the log already exists.
summary: Cloudflare replaced the key-value storage backend inside Durable Objects with SQLite running as an embedded library on the same thread as the application code, so there is no network hop and the post says a query can complete in microseconds and can be issued synchronously without await. Durability comes from output gates, which let writes proceed without blocking but hold the object's response until the relevant writes are confirmed, replacing it with an error and restarting the object if a write fails, so a client never sees a false success. Underneath, the Storage Relay Service, which had already been powering D1 for over a year, intercepts SQLite WAL writes through a custom VFS and batches changes every 10 seconds or 16 MB, whichever comes first, uploading each batch to object storage and writing a new snapshot once the log since the last snapshot exceeds the database size, which caps stored data and restore downloads at 2x the database size. Each commit is also forwarded to five follower machines in different data centers and is confirmed once at least three acknowledge it, and replacing an unreachable host requires reaching three of the five and stopping them from confirming writes for the old instance. Because the log is only marked for deletion 30 days after a snapshot, every SQLite-backed object gets point-in-time recovery to any moment in the last 30 days, on by default, with per-object SQL storage of 1 GB in beta rising to 10 GB at general availability. The post is by Kenton Varda.
title: Zero-latency SQLite storage in every Durable Object

keyTakeaways: Once data lives in shared object storage, replication becomes a metadata problem, so keep the metadata out of local disks and off exclusive locks.
Shared-nothing replication caps how far merge throughput scales, because every replica repeats the same merge work.
Watch active part counts, not just ingest time: two engines can load the same data in similar time and leave wildly different merge debt.
Applying pending mutations on the fly at SELECT time makes updates visible immediately and defers the rewrite to background merges.
Faster background merges make mutations cheaper too, because the rewrite they depend on finishes sooner.
summary: ClickHouse Cloud keeps table data in shared object storage, so the team built SharedMergeTree as a drop-in replacement for ReplicatedMergeTree in which servers share the same physical data and coordinate purely through metadata held in ClickHouse Keeper, with new servers subscribing to metadata changes and caching them locally rather than taking the exclusive Keeper locks that the older zero-copy replication path required. To measure the difference the team loaded about 26 billion WikiStat records from roughly 4,300 compressed files onto clusters of 3, 10, 20 and 80 nodes with 30 CPU cores and 120 GB RAM each. Both engines produced about 23 thousand initial parts of roughly 10 MB, but on 10 nodes ingest times differed by only 19 seconds while ReplicatedMergeTree finished with more than three times as many active parts, about 15 thousand against about 4 thousand, and took about twice as long to merge down; on 20 nodes its replication queue took almost 45 minutes to drain. On 80 nodes, which only SharedMergeTree could use, inserting 26 billion rows finished in 67 seconds, which the post reports as 388 million rows per second. The post also covers lightweight updates, enabled with apply_mutations_on_fly set to 1, which apply pending update expressions at SELECT time so results appear immediately while background merges materialize them later. The author is Tom Schreiber.
title: ClickHouse Cloud boosts performance with SharedMergeTree and Lightweight Updates

keyTakeaways: If storage keeps the WAL history instead of overwriting pages, branching and point-in-time reads fall out of the same mechanism.
Serve reads by finding the newest page image at or before the requested LSN and replaying the WAL records on top of it.
Split immutable files into delta layers that store only changed keys and image layers that snapshot a key range, then compact between them.
A garbage collection horizon is what lets an append-only history stay bounded in cost.
Separating compute from storage lets you shut an idle database down and reattach a fresh compute node to existing storage instead of restoring data.
summary: Neon co-founder Heikki Linnakangas walks through the storage engine behind Neon's serverless Postgres, whose two cornerstones are separating compute from storage and never overwriting stored data. Compute streams WAL to three safekeeper nodes that provide durability through a Paxos-like consensus algorithm, and the safekeepers feed pageservers that reorganize the stream into immutable layer files and upload them to Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage; incoming WAL is buffered in memory and flushed to a new layer file once 1 GB has accumulated. Keys are a relation ID plus block number and values are either an 8 KB page or a WAL record, stored as delta layers that hold only the keys changed over an LSN range and image layers that snapshot a key range at a single LSN. A read carries an LSN, and the pageserver walks layers from that block and LSN until it finds an image, then replays the WAL records on top, while background compaction reshuffles layers to keep lookups fast and garbage collection drops layers older than a horizon. Because nothing is overwritten, branches are copy-on-write: a branch stores its own incoming WAL and falls back to the parent for unmodified data, and an inactive database is shut down after five minutes with a reconnect attaching a new compute node to the existing storage rather than restoring a backup.
title: Deep dive into Neon storage engine

keyTakeaways: Replacing a dependency can be about severity, not count: a handful of storage bugs can each be catastrophic.
A cross-language boundary costs more than call overhead, because it blinds your profiler and tempts you to duplicate logic on both sides.
Owning a storage engine is cheaper when you only implement the feature set your database actually uses.
Bidirectional on-disk compatibility with the engine you are replacing is what makes the rollout reversible.
Metamorphic testing across many predefined and randomly generated configurations is how you find the incompatibilities a unit test will not.
summary: Peter Mattis explains why Cockroach Labs wrote Pebble, a RocksDB-inspired key-value store in Go, to replace RocksDB underneath CockroachDB. The reasons were severity rather than volume of bugs, including a compaction bug that caused an infinite cycle of compactions for a single sstable, performance gaps in RocksDB's first range-deletion implementation that the team upstreamed fixes for, and RocksDB not considering range deletions when choosing compactions, which forced CockroachDB to add a Compactor workaround. Code size and language boundary mattered too: RocksDB had grown from LevelDB's roughly 30 thousand lines to over 350 thousand, Go profiling tools could not introspect C++ or show C++ stack traces, and the team had duplicated some Go logic in C++ to avoid frequent crossings. Pebble is described as a bit over 45 thousand lines of code plus another 45 thousand lines of tests, targets bidirectional on-disk compatibility with RocksDB 6.2.1, and was validated with metamorphic tests running each instance against 19 predefined and 10 randomly generated configurations, which caught bugs such as a signed versus unsigned 8-bit extension that produced different bloom filter hashes for keys containing a high-bit byte. The post says Pebble meets or exceeds RocksDB across the six standard YCSB workloads, with a large delta on workload C attributed to better concurrency in Pebble's block and table cache that became muted at the CockroachDB level; it shipped as opt-in in 20.1 and became the default in 20.2.
title: Introducing Pebble: A RocksDB Inspired Key-Value Store Written in Go

keyTakeaways: Columnar storage is what makes compression possible, because a codec can only exploit similarity within one contiguous column.
Sort order is a compression knob: sorting by host then timestamp reported up to about 40 percent savings, while timestamp first gave 10 percent or less.
Stop storing what you can reconstruct, which is the whole idea behind synthetic _source and later work on rebuilding _id from doc values.
Pick encodings per column rather than globally, since delta, GCD, run-length and bit-packing each win on different data shapes.
On small documents the bookkeeping fields can dominate, and the post notes _id and _seq_no can exceed half the index size.
summary: Luca Wintergerst traces more than a decade of Elasticsearch storage work to explain how LogsDB shrinks log indices, starting from the fact that Lucene keeps the same field values in up to four structures: the inverted index, _source, doc values and BKD trees. Doc values store a field as a column, which lets per-column codecs apply delta encoding, GCD encoding, run-length encoding and bit-packing; the post works a four-timestamp example from 128 raw bits down to 59 with delta and 39 with GCD, and shows sparse doc values from Lucene 7.0 being 81 percent smaller than dense, 24 bytes against 128, for a field populated in 2 of 16 documents. Key milestones include synthetic _source plus index sorting cutting time-series metrics storage by up to 70 percent in 8.7, a custom TSDB doc values codec taking a kubernetes.pod.name column from 110 MB to 7.25 MB, ZSTD replacing DEFLATE in 8.16 for about 12 percent smaller stored fields and about 14 percent higher indexing throughput, route_on_sort_fields adding about 20 percent savings for a 1 to 4 percent ingest penalty in 8.18, and pattern_text cutting message field storage by up to 50 percent for repetitive logs. On Elastic's nightly benchmark, Enterprise mode produced a 37.5 GB index from data that takes 161.9 GB without LogsDB, which the post calls a 77 percent reduction from a single setting, and throughput rose from roughly 25 thousand to roughly 35 thousand documents per second since the Tech Preview. Elastic's summary puts the general range at 50 to 75 percent smaller indices, against the up to 65 percent claimed at GA.
title: Elasticsearch over the years: how LogsDB cuts index size by up to 75% at no throughput cost

keyTakeaways: Treat internally generated config files as untrusted input and validate size and shape before loading them.
A query without an explicit database filter is a latent bug waiting for a permissions change to expose it.
Alternating good and bad artifacts on a five minute refresh look like an attack, which sends responders down the wrong path.
Preallocated limits plus an unwrap on the error path turn a data problem into a process panic.
Error reporting and debug tooling must be bounded, since enhancing uncaught errors consumed CPU and added latency.
summary: Cloudflare published its own analysis of the November 18, 2025 outage, which it says began at 11:20 UTC and was not caused by any attack. A permissions change at 11:05 UTC made tables in the r0 database visible to a user, and because the query that builds the Bot Management feature file did not filter on database name, it started returning duplicate rows and roughly doubled the file size. The core proxy module preallocates memory for a cap of 200 runtime features while only about 60 were in use, so the oversized file tripped an unwrap in the FL2 Rust worker and returned HTTP 5xx; customers still on the older FL proxy instead got a bot score of zero for all traffic. Because the file regenerated every five minutes and only updated ClickHouse nodes produced the bad version, good and bad files alternated and the team first chased a suspected hyper-scale DDoS, helped along by the coincidental failure of the externally hosted status page. Main impact ended at 14:30 UTC once a known good file was propagated and all services were resolved by 17:06 UTC; remediation names hardening ingestion of Cloudflare generated config like user input, more global kill switches, bounding core dumps and error reports, and reviewing error paths in every core proxy module.
title: Cloudflare outage on November 18, 2025

keyTakeaways: A 43 second partition produced 24 hours of degradation, so recovery time is governed by data reconciliation, not by the fault duration.
Consensus based topology managers must be fenced from promoting a primary across a region boundary.
Choosing data integrity over fast recovery is a decision worth making explicitly and early.
Backlogs need their own capacity plan, since millions of queued hooks and a TTL expiry can cause a second loss event.
Restore time depends on backup frequency and where backups live, with four hour backups and multi terabyte clusters setting the floor.
summary: Jason Warner wrote up the October 21, 2018 incident in which GitHub was degraded for 24 hours and 11 minutes. Maintenance to replace failing 100G optical equipment severed the US East Coast hub from the primary East Coast data center for 43 seconds, during which Orchestrator, which manages MySQL topology over Raft, formed a quorum from West Coast and public cloud nodes and failed clusters over to West Coast primaries. East Coast writes from that window had not replicated, so the two sides diverged, and once the application tier started writing to the new primaries the clusters could not be safely failed back; on one of the busiest clusters 954 writes fell inside the affected window and the West Coast had ingested about 40 minutes of writes. The team paused webhook delivery and Pages builds at 23:19 UTC to protect data and restored from backups taken every four hours from remote blob storage, with clusters ranging from hundreds of gigabytes to nearly five terabytes; all primaries were back East at 11:12 UTC on October 22 and the status went green at 23:03 UTC after draining a backlog of over five million hook events and 80,000 Pages builds, with about 200,000 webhook payloads dropped for exceeding an internal TTL. Remediation names fencing Orchestrator against cross region promotion, per component status reporting, an active active active multi data center effort, and validating failure assumptions through fault injection and chaos tooling.
title: October 21 post-incident analysis

keyTakeaways: Observability must not share a failure domain with the thing it observes, or you lose dashboards exactly when you need them.
Autoscaling can make an overload worse when failing health checks recycle hosts that were merely slow.
The provisioning path is a capacity dependency of its own and deserves load testing at the largest scale-up you can imagine.
Predictable traffic events such as the first working day after a holiday justify asking a provider to pre-scale.
Panic mode, retries and circuit breaking turned an outage into degradation while capacity came back.
summary: Laura Nolan explains how Slack went down on the morning of January 4, 2021, the first heavy working day after the holidays, when client caches were cold and traffic jumped. An AWS Transit Gateway linking Slack VPCs did not scale fast enough and began dropping packets, which raised latency between the web tier and its backends; a routine traffic mini-peak at 7:00am PST then saturated the web tier, and at 6:57am only 99 percent of messages were sent successfully against a normal rate above 99.999 percent. Scaling up tried to add 1,200 servers between 7:01am and 7:15am, but the provision-service hit the Linux open files limit and an AWS quota, so most instances never became usable while broken instances consumed autoscaling group capacity, and the team had to disable downscaling to stop healthy hosts being recycled. Debugging was harder because the dashboarding and alerting service ran in a different VPC from its database and therefore depended on the same Transit Gateways, so engineers fell back to internal consoles, raw metric queries, command line tools and logs. Provisioning recovered around 8:15am, enough hosts were serving by 9:15am with panic mode and circuit breaking absorbing the rest, and the network returned to normal at 10:40am after AWS manually raised Transit Gateway capacity in all Availability Zones; the fixes name moving dashboard instances into the same VPC as their database, routinely load testing provision-service, requesting preemptive Transit Gateway capacity after the next holiday season, and retuning health checks and autoscaling.
title: Slack's Outage on January 4th 2021

keyTakeaways: Running every backend service against one Consul cluster made a single subsystem a company wide single point of failure.
A newly enabled feature can change contention behavior days later under a different load mix, so correlate incidents with recent config flips, not just deploys.
Append only stores that never shrink can make small writes enormous, as a 4.2GB log holding 489MB of data showed.
Telemetry that depends on the system it monitors goes dark in the only incident where you need it.
Systems tuned for incremental deploys often cannot cold start, which adds hours to recovery.
summary: Roblox published a joint analysis with HashiCorp of the roughly 73 hour outage from October 28 to October 31, 2021, affecting a service with 50 million daily players running on over 18,000 servers and 170,000 containers. The trouble began with slow Vault calls and one Consul server at high CPU, and median Consul KV write latency rose from under 300ms to about 2 seconds; the team replaced hardware, moved to 128 core NVMe machines, reset from a snapshot and cut non-essential Consul usage, and none of it held. The real cause was a Consul streaming feature enabled on a traffic routing service on October 27, whose use of fewer Go channels created contention that blocked writes under heavy concurrent read and write load, made worse by dual socket NUMA servers; a second factor was BoltDB, where snapshots removed Raft log entries but never shrank the file, leaving a 7.8MB freelist with nearly a million free page IDs that was rewritten on every write, turning 16kB appends into far larger ones and producing TCP zero window back pressure. Disabling streaming on October 30 at 15:51 returned median KV write latency to 300ms, Consul and the cache layer, which serves about 1 billion requests per second at peak, were healthy by 61 hours in, and players were readmitted in roughly 10 percent increments by DNS steering until full access returned at 16:45 on October 31. Remediation names breaking the telemetry dependency on Consul, adding Consul and BoltDB visibility with early warning alerts, sharding critical services onto dedicated Consul clusters, replacing BoltDB with bbolt, a geographically separate data center, and redesigning cache deployment for cold starts.
title: Roblox Return to Service 10/28-10/31 2021

keyTakeaways: Regions are only independent if their update channels and maintenance windows are independent too.
An automatic security update plus a shared 06:00 UTC window turned five regions into one failure domain.
Latent interactions surface on restart, not on boot, so fresh and rebooted nodes hid the bug entirely.
Mass node replacement runs into cloud provider rate limits, which belongs in the recovery plan.
Recovery order matters: control plane first, then live ingestion, then historical backfill.
summary: Alexis Le-Quoc wrote the first part of Datadog's analysis of the March 8, 2023 outage, which started at 06:03 UTC and took down customer access in five regions at once: US1, EU1, US3, US4 and US5. At 06:00 UTC an automatically applied systemd security update on Ubuntu 22.04 restarted systemd-networkd, which deleted routes that the Cilium CNI plugin had installed, and tens of thousands of nodes went offline between 06:00 and 07:00 UTC. The regions failed together because the base OS image still had a legacy security update channel enabled and the default automatic update window was set to 06:00 to 07:00 UTC, so otherwise unconnected regions were hit simultaneously; the bug had never shown up on fresh or rebooted nodes because systemd-networkd starts before the CNI installs its rules during a normal boot. Internal monitoring alerted about three minutes in, a public incident was posted at 06:31 UTC, web access was restored at 09:13 UTC, all services were operational in all regions by 08:58 UTC on March 9, and the incident closed at 06:25 UTC on March 10 once historical data had been backfilled, with the response run by an emergency operations center of 10 senior leaders, about 70 local incident commanders and 450 to 750 responders over four shifts. The named fixes are disabling the legacy update channel in the affected regions, changing the systemd-networkd configuration so a restart leaves the routing table untouched, and auditing the rest of the infrastructure for other legacy channels.
title: 2023-03-08 Incident: Infrastructure connectivity issue affecting multiple regions

keyTakeaways: Request coalescing in a CDN can convert one slow origin fetch into a synchronized retry storm when it finally completes.
A canary that watches error rates is blind to requests that simply never finish, so add a completion signal.
Asset fetches need timeouts, or a stalled download silently accumulates clients waiting to pile on at once.
A known performance bug in a telemetry library is a reliability bug once traffic reaches 3x normal peak.
You cannot autoscale out of a cascade while load keeps arriving, so blocking traffic at the edge is what lets new tasks start.
summary: Brendan Humphreys and colleagues published Canva's report on the November 12, 2024 outage, during which canva.com was unavailable from about 9:08 to 10:00 AM UTC. A new editor version deployed at 8:47 AM made clients fetch over 100 new static assets through Cloudflare just as the Singapore to Ashburn path degraded, with 90th percentile time to first byte up by over 1700 percent and packet loss peaking around 66 percent, which Cloudflare attributed to a stale traffic management rule sending IPv6 traffic over public transit. One JavaScript chunk for the object panel took 20 minutes to complete, and Cloudflare's cache stream feature coalesced over 270,000 user requests onto that single fetch; because none of them completed, no errors were recorded and the canary system never aborted the deploy. When the file finally landed at 9:07 AM every waiting device loaded the object panel at once, producing about 1.5 million requests per second against the API Gateway, roughly 3x typical peak, and a recent telemetry library change that re-registered metrics under a third party lock on every recorded value throttled the event loop threads; off-heap memory growth then let the Linux OOM killer terminate all running containers within the first two minutes. Recovery came from a Cloudflare firewall rule at 9:29 AM blocking all CDN traffic to the API Gateway so fresh tasks could start, followed by gradual restoration beginning with Australian users under strict rate limits, and remediation names load shedding rules, higher baseline task count and memory, regular load testing, asset fetch timeouts, page load completion as a second canary signal, and patching the telemetry locking bug with multithreaded benchmarks.
title: Canva incident report: API Gateway outage

keyTakeaways: Repeated parse and marshal steps, not storage, were the bottleneck in their logging pipeline at this scale.
A byte for byte native format copy cut the CPU cost of shipping logs by more than an order of magnitude, by their numbers.
Pull based scraping degrades gracefully: scrapers run at a steady rate and backfill by rescraping windows instead of dropping events.
Storing raw wide rows and aggregating at query time avoids the cardinality trade-offs of pre-aggregated metrics.
Hashing each source schema and unioning versions with a Merge table lets the pipeline absorb schema drift without migrations.
summary: Rory Crispin and Dale McDiarmid describe how ClickHouse grew LogHouse, the internal platform that monitors ClickHouse Cloud, from about 19 PiB and 37 trillion rows to over 100 PB uncompressed and nearly 500 trillion rows, which they say also saved millions by replacing a Datadog bill. The old path was wasteful: a server wrote JSON to stdout, the kubelet persisted it, and an OpenTelemetry collector parsed, marshalled and converted it to OTel format before converting again into ClickHouse native format, flattening native types along the way, and per node agents hit CPU and memory limits during spikes and dropped lines. They estimated that pushing 20 million rows per second through OTel without loss would need roughly 8,000 CPU cores, so they built SysEx, a scraper that runs SELECT queries against source system tables and streams the result into LogHouse in native format with no intermediate decoding, assigning pods to replicas over a hash ring and reading a sliding window about five minutes behind real time. By their numbers OTel collectors used over 800 cores to ship 2 million logs per second while SysEx uses about 70 cores for 37 million logs per second, and SysEx now holds 93.6 PB and 431 trillion rows against 14.5 PB and 16.7 trillion for OTel. OTel is kept deliberately for stdout and stderr when a service is crash looping and system tables cannot be queried, now at info level and above, and the team argues for wide rows with full context plus query time aggregation rather than Prometheus style series that would explode cardinality across tens of thousands of pod names.
title: Scaling our Observability platform beyond 100 Petabytes by embracing wide events and replacing OTel

keyTakeaways: Gossip based cluster membership becomes a dominant cost at scale: ring propagation alone burned about 2,500 CPU cores before optimization.
Define SLOs for the load test first, then hunt the bottleneck that breaks them.
TSDB index size limits from 32 bit offsets cap how large a single compacted block can be, which forces sharded compaction.
Synchronous head chunk flushes created huge p99 latency spikes, fixed with jitter plus an asynchronous write queue.
Rollout time is a scalability property too, cut from about 50 hours to under 30 minutes with zone aware replication.
summary: Marco Pracucci documents how Grafana Labs load tested Grafana Mimir with a single tenant at 1 billion active series, meaning series that received a sample in the last 20 minutes, ingesting about 3 billion series at replication factor 3 and roughly 50 million samples per second at a 20 second scrape interval. The test ramped from 200 million to 1 billion series over several weeks on a cluster of about 1,500 replicas, about 7,000 CPU cores and 30 TiB of RAM, against SLOs of 99.9 percent of writes under 10 seconds and 99.9 percent of reads succeeding with average query time under 2 seconds. Each of the roughly 1,500 replicas spent 1.6 to 1.9 cores purely propagating hash ring changes, about 2,500 cores in total, which optimizations to the receive path, state merging, allocations and probe settings reduced by more than 90 percent, and a memberlist bug where corrupted packets caused gigabyte sized buffer allocations and OOMKills was fixed and upstreamed to HashiCorp. Other fixes were a split and merge compactor running on 150 replicas so all compactions finished within 12 hours and no uncompacted block was queried, query sharding and time splitting that cut average execution of high cardinality queries by about 10x with one example going from 37.7s to 3.9s, jitter plus an asynchronous write queue for ingester head chunk flushes that dropped the p99 peak from 45s to 3s, disabling TSDB isolation for a 90 percent ingester p99 reduction, and zone aware replication with a rollout operator that took a 600 ingester rollout from about 50 hours to under 30 minutes.
title: How we scaled our new Prometheus TSDB Grafana Mimir to 1 billion active series

keyTakeaways: Streaming compression beats one-shot compression when payloads are small, because context carries across messages.
Dark launching a codec on a slice of production traffic and throwing the output away lets you iterate in days instead of waiting on client release cycles.
Trained dictionaries helped tiny events but not the common ones, so the team shipped without them rather than pay the complexity.
The biggest single win was protocol shape, not compression: sending deltas instead of full snapshots.
Measure per event type; a codec that looks worse on average may win once configured correctly.
summary: Discord spent roughly six months cutting the bandwidth its clients use on the gateway WebSocket, which had been zlib compressed since late 2017. Switching to zstandard only paid off after the team forked the ezstd Erlang bindings to add streaming compression and contributed it upstream: with streaming, MESSAGE_CREATE payloads fell from 270 bytes to 166 bytes and the compression ratio rose from about 6 to almost 10, while compression time dropped from about 100 to about 45 microseconds. Trained dictionaries were tested on about 120,000 messages and dropped, since READY improved only from a 6.4 to a 6.63 ratio and MESSAGE_CREATE got worse. The second change, Passive Sessions V2, replaced full snapshots of channels, members and voice members with deltas: that one event type had been 35.61 percent of gateway traffic despite being about 2 percent of dispatches, and it fell to roughly 5 percent. Together zstd plus Passive Sessions V2 cut client gateway bandwidth by almost 40 percent.
title: How Discord Reduced Websocket Traffic by 40%

keyTakeaways: Routing invalidation through a core data center makes purge latency a function of how far the customer is from that core.
Lazy purge trades storage for simplicity: you must keep purge history longer than the maximum eviction age, which steals disk from the cache itself.
A per-machine index of hostnames, tags and URLs turns an impossible disk scan into a lookup.
Checking a pending purge queue at cache hit time stops stale content from being served before deletion finishes.
Benchmark with real customer requests, not synthetic load, and store per-request timings so you can compute quantiles.
summary: Cloudflare rebuilt flexible cache purge, meaning purge by tag, hostname and prefix, to remove the dependency on core data centers. The old design sent purges through a core, distributed them with Quicksilver in a spoke and hub model, and used lazy purge, which left matching files on disk and compared timestamps at request time. The new coreless design accepts a purge in any data center and fans it out to every machine, where a Rust service called CacheDB, built on RocksDB and talking to the cache proxy over Unix domain sockets, maintains indexes on hostnames, cache-tags and URLs plus a local purge queue; on a cache hit the proxy checks that queue, so purged content stops being served immediately. Measuring real customer purges in August 2024 against May 2022, global P50 latency fell from 1,570ms to 149ms, a 90.5 percent improvement, with Eastern North America at 119ms and Africa at 303ms. Single-file purge sits at a 234ms P50 against a stated goal of getting under 200ms, and deleting files eagerly instead of lazily also cut storage needs by about 10x.
title: Instant Purge: invalidating cached content in under 150ms

keyTakeaways: Unsharded Redis PubSub broadcasts to every cluster node, so throughput falls as you add nodes; one big single node can beat a cluster.
Use streams for control events that must not be lost and pub/sub for high-volume positional updates that can be dropped.
Serialization and client flush batching were each worth about 30 percent CPU, which is cheaper than re-architecting.
Deploys that close every WebSocket turn reconnection cost into an overload problem, because new instances take all new connections.
Peer-to-peer removes the backend from the data path, but roughly half of connections still need a relay, so budget for TURN.
summary: Canva's collaboration team describes two generations of the system that moves live mouse pointers between people editing the same design, built against a target of 3 position updates per second per user for up to 50 users, with a long-term goal of 60 updates per second, a 20x increase. The first design used WebSockets to stateless backend instances with Redis as the broker, Redis Streams for join and leave control data because of its delivery guarantees and Redis PubSub for the pointer updates; it reached 100 percent of collaborative editing sessions, hundreds of thousands of simultaneous clients and about 100,000 pointer updates per second at a peak of 27 percent CPU on a single Redis instance. Because Redis 6.2 lacked the sharded PubSub added in 7.0, messages went to every cluster node, so the team moved PubSub onto one m6g.8xlarge node; switching from JSON to protobuf cut backend CPU by about 30 percent and disabling per-command auto-flushing in Lettuce cut Redis CPU by about another 30 percent. Since a single Redis node could not carry 60 updates per second, the second milestone moved pointer traffic to WebRTC data channels in a full mesh, where 10 users means 9 connections each, with Canva's existing WebSocket infrastructure as the signaling server. About 50 percent of those connections end up relayed through TURN, and clients that cannot open a channel with any active peer fall back to WebSocket, with duplicate updates ignored by sender ID.
title: Real-time mouse pointers

keyTakeaways: Config reloads are the hidden cost of long-lived connections: old processes must linger for hours to let connections drain, then be reaped.
Dynamic endpoint discovery removes reloads from the backend-change path entirely.
Running a full parallel stack doubles infrastructure spend but makes every rollout step reversible.
Generate load balancer config from code with validation, not raw templates, and test by generating other teams' configs to catch regressions.
Old load balancer config encodes accidental behavior that customers depend on, so plan to preserve it rather than clean it up mid-migration.
summary: Slack moved the WebSocket tier that carries millions of simultaneously connected clients from HAProxy to Envoy. The driver was operational: backend endpoint changes were rendered into HAProxy config and applied with a reload, each reload spawned new processes, and old processes had to be kept alive for many hours so long-lived WebSockets could drain, which forced the team to reap stale processes and rate limit reloads. Envoy's dynamically configured clusters and endpoints avoid reloads when endpoints change, and it can hot restart without dropping connections while copying stats from parent to child; the team also wanted zone-aware routing, outlier detection and panic routing, which helped during the January 4, 2021 outage. Config is generated from custom Chef libraries as a per-host singleton, validated with Envoy's validate mode before install, and traffic was shifted with NS1 weighted DNS between the HAProxy and Envoy load balancer names, at 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent in early regions and later 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent within two days per region instead of about one region per week. The migration ran a parallel Envoy stack, which doubled AWS resource usage, took about six months, and finished globally with zero customer impact.
title: Migrating Millions of Concurrent Websockets to Envoy

keyTakeaways: Terminating TLS and TCP close to the user shortens the round trip, so transport ramps up to full throughput sooner.
Advertising every prefix from every PoP creates asymmetric paths; scoping prefixes per metro makes each metro a failure domain you can drain.
Equalize transit capacity across PoPs so a drained metro can actually fail over to nearby capacity.
Use flow data to find the top networks sitting behind your transit providers, then peer with them directly.
Upload paths can benefit more than download paths from edge proximity, so measure both.
summary: Dropbox describes how its edge network went from a US-only footprint of two data center regions and five PoPs in 2014, peering with about 100 networks and running almost entirely on tier-1 transit, to 14 PoPs across seven countries and three continents by the end of 2016, with edge capacity in the terabits. Along the way the team migrated its internal routing protocol from OSPF to IS-IS, implemented MPLS traffic engineering to balance backbone utilization, and replaced the practice of advertising all public prefixes from every PoP with a metro-scoped BGP community scheme that tags prefixes by origin, route type and scope so an individual metro can be withdrawn and drained. A custom edge proxy stack built from IPVS and NGINX handles user-facing TLS and TCP setup; Dropbox evaluated CDNs and other cloud products first and judged a custom build the better fit, given that more than 90 percent of user data lives on its own infrastructure and about 75 percent of its more than 500 million users are outside the US. NetFlow analysis identified the top networks behind transit providers, and by the end of 2016 about 30 percent of traffic had moved to peering across more than 200 newly added ASNs. After the edge proxies went in, Dropbox reports median download speeds up about 40 percent and median uploads up about 90 percent in Europe, with median downloads doubling and uploads tripling in Japan, and says some users saw sync speeds increase by as much as 300 percent.
title: Evolution of Dropbox's Edge Network

keyTakeaways: Treat the open persistent connection itself as the online signal, so you do not need a separate online event.
Going online is easy; going offline is the hard case, because nothing fires an event when a client simply disappears.
A heartbeat with TTL plus a delayed trigger at heartbeat interval plus a margin absorbs network jitter without flapping the indicator.
Hash the member ID to a consistent node so heartbeats and the trigger for one member land in the same place and you avoid duplicate offline events.
One lightweight actor per online member scales to millions on a small thread pool, but deploys must wait out the trigger window before restarting.
summary: LinkedIn explains how it shows the green online indicator for roughly 500 million members, built on the Play Framework and the Akka Actor Model on top of the real-time delivery platform, a publish and subscribe system it had built the previous year for instant messaging that streams events to web and mobile clients over persistent connections. Because an open connection means the member is online, the platform only needs to publish presence changes to subscribers who are viewing that member. For each connected member the platform emits a heartbeat every d seconds into a distributed key value store whose entries expire after d plus epsilon, which keeps a member who drops and reconnects quickly from flickering offline. Offline detection comes from a delayed trigger at d plus two epsilon, implemented as one Akka actor per online member that schedules a publish-offline message to itself, with the d2 load balancer hashing on member ID so heartbeats for a member reach the same node and duplicate triggers are avoided; nodes are drained by waiting that same window before restarting. At the reported scale thousands of members go online or offline per second, millions are online at any moment, each node handles about 1.8K QPS, and presence changes reach subscribers in under 200ms at p99.
title: Now You See Me, Now You Don't: LinkedIn's Real-Time Presence Platform

keyTakeaways: Optimizing p90 and p99 can miss the product feeling slow, so track the share of navigations that land in an instant bucket instead.
Check whether revisit rates can even support a client cache before building one; the viability threshold here was about a 30 percent hit rate.
Stale-while-revalidate on the client buys instant renders at the cost of a measurable, bounded divergence from the server.
Prefetching high-intent records on low-priority workers, behind rate limits and circuit breakers, moved the hit ratio from about 33 percent to about 96 percent.
A service worker extends a client cache to full page loads by letting the server return a thin shell when the payload is already local.
summary: GitHub rebuilt how the Issues page loads, measuring with an internal metric called Highest Priority Content that is aligned with Largest Contentful Paint and bucketed as instant under 200ms, fast under 1000ms and slow at or above 1000ms. At baseline 57.6 percent of issue page views were hard navigations and 37.5 percent were React soft navigations, and the team deliberately shifted focus from tail percentiles to the share of navigations in the fast and instant buckets. The first step added an IndexedDB client cache with stale-while-revalidate, which raised instant React navigations from 4 percent to about 22 percent at an observed hit ratio of about 33 percent and a server-to-cache divergence of about 4.7 percent; adding preheating of high-intent issue references on rate-limited low-priority workers, plus an in-memory cache in front of IndexedDB, pushed the hit ratio to about 96 percent and instant navigations to about 30 percent overall and up to about 70 percent for React navigations. The second step put a service worker in front of hard and Turbo navigations so a cached payload lets the server return a thin HTML shell instead of a full server-rendered response, with route-based code splitting, dynamic route preloading and hover prefetching to offset the JavaScript cost that then dominates. Across all issue page traffic, P10 went from about 600ms to 70ms, P25 from about 800ms to 120ms, P50 from about 1,200ms to 700ms, P75 from 1,800ms to 1,400ms and P90 from 2,400ms to 2,100ms.
title: From latency to instant: Modernizing GitHub Issues navigation performance

keyTakeaways: Measure real access patterns per bucket before changing storage class, because lifecycle rules set years earlier may never have been validated.
Transition fees scale with object count while savings scale with bytes stored, so average object size decides the payback period.
Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill a 128 KB minimum per object, which makes very small objects cheaper to leave in Standard.
Canva prioritized buckets averaging 400 KB or more per object to get return on investment inside six months.
summary: Canva keeps over 230 PB in Amazon S3, with its largest single bucket at 45 PB, and had lifecycle rules moving user designs into Standard-IA after 30 days without ever measuring whether that paid off. The team used S3 Storage Class Analysis per bucket to chart bytes stored and retrieval rates by object age, found retrieval drops off sharply after about 15 days, and targeted S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which stores more cheaply than Standard-IA while keeping millisecond reads. Because transitions cost $0.02 per 1,000 objects against an inventory of over 300 billion objects, moving everything would have cost more than $6 million, so they ranked buckets by average object size and only migrated those paying back within six months. They applied lifecycle policies bucket by bucket and moved nearly 80 billion objects in about two days at a one time cost of over $1.6 million, putting roughly 130 PB of the 230 PB into Glacier Instant Retrieval. Canva reports saving about $300,000 per month, or roughly $3.6 million a year, with the investment turning positive within a few months.
title: How Canva saves millions annually in Amazon S3 costs

keyTakeaways: Git pairs candidate files for delta compression using only the last 16 characters of their paths, so directory layout can quietly inflate a repository.
Internationalization files that carry the language code early in the path defeat that heuristic and make routine translation updates balloon pack files.
On hosted Git a local repack does not persist, because transfer packs are built server side, so the fix had to run on the provider's servers.
Dropbox reports the repo going from 87 GB to 20 GB, a 77% reduction, and clones from over an hour to under 15 minutes in many cases.
summary: Dropbox's server monorepo had reached 87 GB and was growing about 20 to 60 MB a day with spikes above 150 MB, putting it months from GitHub Enterprise Cloud's 100 GB hard limit while a fresh clone took over an hour and CI jobs paid that cost repeatedly. The team traced the bloat to Git's delta compression, which pairs files for comparison by the last 16 characters of their paths, and Dropbox stores language codes early in its i18n paths, so Git kept comparing files across different languages and produced oversized deltas. An experimental path walk flag repacked a local copy from the low 80s GB into the low 20s GB but conflicted with GitHub's server side bitmaps and delta islands, so the fix became a tuned server side repack with depth and window both set to 250, which took about nine hours on a mirror and brought 84 G down to 20 G. A test mirror fell from 78 GB to 18 GB with only minor movement in fetch latency at the tail, after which GitHub applied the repack in production one replica per day across a week. The published results are a 77% size reduction, clone times under 15 minutes, no regression in fetch duration, push success rate or API latency, plus an updated i18n workflow and a recurring job that tracks repo size, growth rate and clone time.
title: Reducing our monorepo size to improve developer velocity

keyTakeaways: Several compounding changes beat one rewrite: compression, local instance storage, tiered storage and newer hardware each took a slice of the bill.
Tiered storage keeps older data once in S3 at 2 cents per GB instead of on all three replicas, which cost 24 cents per ingested GB on SSD.
Measuring cost per MB of ingested data, not cluster size, is what made each change comparable.
Honeycomb reports about 10x data growth over two years for only 20% more Kafka total cost of ownership, an 87% cumulative drop in cost per MB.
summary: Honeycomb runs its ingest path on Kafka behind a 99.99% availability objective, and the post walks through several years of changes aimed at cost per megabyte of incoming data rather than raw cluster size. The fleet moved from 16 c5.xlarge brokers on gp2 EBS at 10 cents per GB month to i3en brokers using local NVMe at 8 cents per GB month, picked up Zstandard compression, and adopted Confluent tiered storage so only the latest two to four hours sits on local disk while older segments go to S3 at 2 cents per GB instead of being replicated three times on SSD. In late 2021 the team tested Graviton2 based im4gn.4xlarge brokers, which ran at 30% peak CPU and 20% disk utilization, replicated twice as fast as i3en.3xlarge, and cost 14% more than i3en.3xlarge while being 43% cheaper than i3en.6xlarge. Honeycomb attributes roughly 25% of its savings to Zstandard, 20% to moving from c5 with gp2 to reserved i3en, 65% to tiered storage and 43% to the i3en to im4gn switch, noting that these compound rather than add. The headline result is about 10x growth in data volume over two years for a 20% rise in Kafka total cost of ownership, which the authors describe as an 87% cumulative reduction in cost per MB ingested, with no engineer working on Kafka full time.
title: Scaling Kafka at Honeycomb

keyTakeaways: Choosing a storage engine built for aggregation beat trying to stream aggregate 6M events per second through Flink.
Shrinking a record from 1630 bytes of Cap'n Proto to 36.74 bytes columnar turned a year of retention from an estimated $28M into about $1.9M at a $100 per TiB basis.
Lowering index granularity on the aggregated table from 8192 to 32 cut query latency 50% and raised throughput about threefold.
Pre-aggregating into a few purpose built tables kept the API fast while the raw request table stayed available for drill down.
summary: Cloudflare's 2014 HTTP analytics pipeline ended in a single PostgreSQL instance with no replicas or backups, fronted by an API that struggled to exceed about 15 queries per second, while traffic grew from under 1M to an average of 6M requests per second with peaks of 8M. A first attempt to aggregate with Apache Flink could not keep up at that ingestion rate, so the team adopted ClickHouse, which another internal team already ran for DNS analytics. The new pipeline is a 36 node ClickHouse cluster with replication factor three fed by 106 Go consumers from Kafka, inserting 11M rows per second across pipelines at about 47 Gbps, and it shrank the per record footprint from 1630 bytes of Cap'n Proto, or 360 bytes with Zstandard, to 36.74 bytes, which cut the estimated one year storage need from 273.93 PiB and $28M to 18.52 PiB and about $1.9M. Tuning mattered as much as the engine: dropping index granularity on the aggregated table from 8192 to 32 cut query latency by 50% and raised throughput about threefold, and a faster map merge in SummingMergeTree improved roughly sevenfold. The result serves over 7M customer domains with 365 days of retention, sustains about 40 queries per second with load tests reaching about 150, and let Cloudflare shut down 12 Citus nodes.
title: HTTP Analytics for 6M requests per second using ClickHouse

keyTakeaways: Swapping the wire format underneath a shared RPC framework can be made close to invisible to application developers.
LinkedIn benchmarked seven candidate formats before picking Protobuf, weighing ecosystem and multi language support alongside raw speed.
Symbol tables plus configuration driven ramps let more than 50,000 endpoints migrate gradually and reversibly.
The authors report up to 60% lower latency for large payload services and about 8% better resource utilization, with no statistically significant regressions.
summary: LinkedIn had standardized on JSON as the serialization format across more than 50,000 Rest.li API endpoints spanning eight languages, and at a scale of billions of member requests a day the text parsing cost and the absence of a compact binary representation had become a measurable tax. The team benchmarked seven alternatives, including Flatbuffers, Cap'n Proto, SMILE, MessagePack, CBOR and Kryo, and chose Protocol Buffers for its wire efficiency, schema evolution story and breadth of language support. They implemented Protobuf as a pluggable Rest.li wire format and rolled it out using symbol tables and configuration based ramps, so the switch was nearly transparent to application developers and could be ramped or reverted per service. The reported outcome is up to 60% lower latency for services with large payloads, about 8% better resource utilization, and average per host throughput gains of 6.25% on response payloads and 1.77% on request payloads, with no statistically significant degradation against JSON in any service.
title: LinkedIn Integrates Protocol Buffers With Rest.li for Improved Microservices Performance

keyTakeaways: Idle ratio is a sharper efficiency target than node count or total spend, because it points straight at the scheduling decision that wasted the money.
Cluster Autoscaler can only pick from predefined node groups, while Karpenter sizes instances to the pending pods and can replace a fleet with a cheaper mix.
Hitting the EKS maximum pods per node limit left nodes roughly half empty, which node group based scaling could not fix.
Weighted provisioners with CPU limits kept existing EC2 Instance Savings Plan commitments useful during the migration.
Grafana Labs reports idleness ratios falling by 50% on average from the migration alone, short of its 15% goal in some clusters.
summary: Some of Grafana Labs' AWS clusters were running north of 40% idle capacity, partly because nodes hit the EKS maximum pods per node limit while roughly half their CPU and memory sat unused, and Cluster Autoscaler could only scale predefined node groups. The team moved every workload except a static node group for critical cluster components onto Karpenter, which provisions instances sized to the pending pods, prefers Spot with On Demand fallback, and consolidates On Demand nodes when a cheaper configuration still fits the workloads. Nodes carry a 30 day time to live so Karpenter expires and replaces them, keeping the fleet churning toward a better fit instead of drifting. To avoid stranding existing EC2 Instance Savings Plan commitments, they ran two provisioners with different weights and CPU limits and let Compute Savings Plans cover the remainder. The authors report that the migration alone cut idleness ratios by 50% on average against a target of 15% that not every cluster reached, and they publish no dollar figure.
title: How Grafana Labs switched to Karpenter to reduce costs and complexities in Amazon EKS

keyTakeaways: Request-count round robin ignores hardware differences, so equal request counts still leave some servers much hotter than others.
A central load balancing service can collect server load reports and publish per-endpoint weights to a routing database that Envoy and gRPC clients already read.
Treating balance as a control problem lets one PID controller per node drive that node toward the fleet average utilization.
Flattening the max over average CPU ratio toward 1.0 is what unlocks fleet shrinkage, because over-provisioning exists to cover the hottest node.
Blending new PID weights with plain round robin behind a percentage gate keeps the migration reversible.
summary: Dropbox describes the latest iteration of Robinhood, the in-house load balancing service it deployed in 2020 to even out load across backend fleets. Clients had been round robining over endpoints from service discovery with no view of server load, and because hardware generations differ, identical request counts left some instances hot, so teams over-provisioned to cover the worst node. Robinhood now runs a PID controller per node with average fleet utilization as the setpoint, publishes normalized endpoint weights into a ZooKeeper or etcd routing database, and lets Envoy and gRPC clients do weighted round robin; services can balance on CPU, in-flight requests, or the maximum of both, and the service skips a weight update whenever more than 15 percent of load reports are missing. The team reports the max over average CPU ratio falling from 1.26 to 1.01 on a large Envoy proxy cluster and from 1.4 to 1.05 on a database frontend cluster, which they describe as 20 percent and 25 percent improvements. Those flatter curves let Dropbox cut fleet size by 25 percent for some of its largest services.
title: What's new with Robinhood, our in-house load balancing service

keyTakeaways: Hive Metastore planning that scales linearly with partition count makes the catalog the bottleneck long before storage is.
Migrating the highest scan frequency and highest API cost tables first pays back the one-time metadata and storage tier spike.
Z-ordering plus Trino data skipping took one navigation dataset from 70 seconds to 6 seconds.
A unified Spark catalog that routes by detected table format removes format-specific prefixes from user queries.
Timestamp semantics shifted in Spark 3.4, so legacy Hive views needed a custom migration workflow and Trino patches.
summary: Grab's data lake held petabytes across billions of S3 objects, mostly Hive Parquet tables managed through a Hive Metastore. Rahul Penti lays out four bottlenecks the team hit: centralized catalog latency with query planning that scaled linearly with partition count, small file fragmentation where ML datasets averaged under 1 MB per file with thousands of files per partition, manual partition registration with no native ACID support, and a catalog that drifted out of sync when S3 changed underneath it. Grab made Apache Iceberg its default table format and rolled it out table by table instead of converting the whole lake, and it built UnifiedSparkCatalog to route operations to the right format-specific catalog for Iceberg, Delta, Hudi, or Hive by detecting the format from metadata properties or path inference. The team reports a high-traffic navigation dataset going from 70 seconds to 6 seconds, roughly 10x, after Z-ordering and Trino data skipping, daily S3 API costs on a heavily queried operations table falling by up to 95 percent with no query changes, and cluster resource usage on a funnel analysis dataset dropping by about half. They also report the snags: zombie locks in the Hive Metastore blocked commits under high load until retries and read timeouts were tuned, a TIMESTAMP_NTZ versus TIMESTAMP_LTZ mismatch in Spark 3.4 broke legacy Hive views, and generating Iceberg metadata caused a one-time storage tier cost spike.
title: Scaling Grab's Data Lake: Our journey to Apache Iceberg adoption

keyTakeaways: Fanning a build out into thousands of tiny jobs pays instance warm-up and cache download cost over and over.
A first-principles estimate of the theoretical floor, about 20 minutes here, tells you how much headroom is actually left.
A 448 CPU machine still took 18 minutes cold, which proved the critical path was bound by single-CPU actions rather than by capacity.
Bazel's remote-download-minimal avoids fetching artifacts nobody needs, but needs retries because of remote cache eviction.
Pre-warmed agents from EBS snapshots cut P95 peak wait for large agents from 40 minutes to 10.
summary: Canva's main repository had a CI problem: in April 2022 an average pull request took about 80 minutes to pass CI and merge, and the worst builds ran up to 3 hours. Marco Lacava and Arpit Sharma trace that to excessive horizontal scaling, where a P90 check-merge build fanned out to roughly 3,000 jobs that each wanted their own EC2 instance and each paid cold cache and warm-up cost, plus non-hermetic script steps that could not be cached or parallelized, against a build graph of over 900K nodes and petabytes of dependency downloads per week. Testing a 448 CPU, 6 TB RAM instance still produced an 18 minute cold build, which showed the critical path was bound by single-CPU actions, so the work went after that path: i4i.8xlarge workers took the slowest job from up to 3 hours to about 15 minutes, Bazel's remote-download-minimal made backend builds about 2x faster and ML builds about 3.3x faster, and the pipeline generator was rewritten in Starlark from many thousands of lines down to a couple hundred. The team reports the backend and ML pipeline v2 cutting average build time from 49 to 35 minutes with steps down from 45 to 16, and accessibility test jobs going from 67,145 across 13,947 commits to roughly one job per commit. Merge CI now lands under 30 minutes and sometimes around 15, though the authors note regressions still happen through downstream dependencies.
title: Faster continuous integration builds at Canva

keyTakeaways: Minting short-lived credentials only after a second engineer approves puts a human in the loop without blocking incident response.
Running the broker in a Nitro enclave lets the parent instance forward TLS without being able to read or tamper with enclave memory.
Gating the KMS Decrypt of seed secrets on an attestation document ties those secrets to one exact measured binary.
Reproducible pure Go enclave images let two security engineers independently confirm the workload hash before a deploy is trusted.
Keeping the broker off the normal platform secret store avoids a cyclic dependency an admin could exploit to bypass approval.
summary: Monzo runs more than 2,500 microservices on a shared platform, where a platform-wide change needs highly privileged credentials whose blast radius is the whole estate, and urgent incident fixes in particular have no automated pipeline, so engineers occasionally need temporary elevated access. Craig Ferguson describes the multi-party authorisation broker Monzo built for this: an engineer runs mpa request for credentials to a target such as an AWS account or a Kubernetes cluster, a second engineer runs mpa review to approve, and the requester then runs mpa fetch to collect short-lived credentials, minted through STS AssumeRole for AWS or OIDC tokens for Kubernetes, with every request logged to the security event pipeline and posted to Slack. The hard part was bootstrapping trust in the broker itself, since the engineers it constrains are the same ones who maintain it, so the broker runs inside an AWS Nitro enclave with no persistent storage and no external network, reachable only over a virtual socket through an Envoy proxy on the parent that forwards TLS without terminating it, and it recovers its long-lived seed secrets through an AWS KMS Decrypt call that only succeeds for an attestation document carrying the expected measurements. The enclave images are reproducible pure Go binaries, with the Nitro SDKs reimplemented in Go to drop hard-to-reproduce toolchain dependencies, so two security engineers independently rebuild and agree on the hash before a version is deployed through the MPA system itself. The team reports the system running in production for over a year and used daily for both routine changes and incident response.
title: Securing admin access to Monzo's platform

keyTakeaways: Sandboxing inference under gvisor is cheap on GPU throughput but expensive on CPU, so a trusted bare-metal process wins back cores.
Pre-allocating a full KV cache per prompt would fit only 4 parallel prompts on an H100, which is why paged allocation is mandatory.
Chunked prefill lets the batcher fill spare batch slots with prompt tokens, turning scattered work into larger Tensor Core matrix multiplications.
JIT-compiling kernels for the specific model and GPU, in parallel with weight loading, hides most of the startup cost.
CPU cost per request matters as much as tokens per second when GPUs are spread across many edge locations.
summary: Cloudflare runs inference on GPUs spread across a network that sits within 50 ms of 95 percent of the Internet-connected population, which makes per-node efficiency the binding constraint rather than raw cluster size. The post describes Infire, an LLM inference engine written in Rust with three parts: an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server built on hyper, a batcher, and the engine itself. Weights are fetched from R2 and cached on the node, then copied to the GPU through page-locked memory and asynchronous CUDA copies across multiple streams while kernels JIT-compile in parallel, so loading Llama-3-8B-Instruct from disk takes just under 4 seconds; the engine uses continuous batching with chunked prefill, a paged KV cache that avoids pre-allocating for the full 128K context, low-level PTX kernels for Hopper GPUs, and per-batch-size CUDA graphs. On a ShareGPT v3 benchmark of 4,000 prompts at concurrency 200 on an H100 NVL, Cloudflare reports Infire at 40.91 requests per second and 17,224 tokens per second at 25 percent CPU load, against vLLM 0.10.0 at 38.38 requests per second and 16,164 tokens per second at 140 percent CPU, and vLLM under gvisor at 37.13 requests per second at 250 percent CPU. The team reports Infire running up to 7 percent faster than vLLM 0.10.0 on unloaded machines and reaching GPU utilization above 80 percent in production, with Flash Attention 3 integration and kernel fusion still in progress.
title: How we built the most efficient inference engine for Cloudflare's network
